skill.name: golang-stretchr-testify
skill.description: Comprehensive guide to stretchr/testify for Golang testing. Covers assert, require, mock, and suite packages in depth. Use when writing tests with testify, creating mocks, setting up test suites, or choosing between assert and require. Covers testify assertions, mock expectations, argument matchers, call verification, suite lifecycle, and advanced patterns like Eventually, JSONEq, and custom matchers. Apply when the codebase imports github.com/stretchr/testify.
skill.summary: Practical guidance for writing reliable Go tests with testify assertions, mocks, suites, and async checks.
skill.author: samber

content.user_title: Write Better Go Tests with Testify
content.value_statement: Testify gives Go developers readable assertions, reliable mocks, and structured suites. This skill helps AI generate and review focused tests with correct failure behavior and expectation checks.
actual_capabilities: Explain when to use assert versus require for Go test preconditions and verifications.
Generate testify assertions for equality, errors, JSON, collections, pointers, and asynchronous polling.
Design testify/mock expectations with matchers, call counts, side effects, and return sequences.
Create testify suites with per-test setup, shared lifecycle hooks, and the required launcher.
Review tests for common testify mistakes and recommend testifylint checks.
limitations: It does not execute Go tests or inspect the target repository without suitable tools and source access.
It does not replace package documentation for version-specific testify behavior.
Generated examples require adaptation to the project interfaces, fixtures, and dependency versions.
It does not guarantee complete coverage or detect every semantic test weakness.

use_cases.title: Add focused unit tests
use_cases.description: Generate readable Go tests with fail-fast preconditions and clear value assertions for new functions.

use_cases.title: Build dependable mocks
use_cases.description: Define mock expectations, argument matchers, call counts, and retry responses for isolated service tests.

use_cases.title: Review existing test suites
use_cases.description: Find assertion-order errors, missing expectation verification, incorrect suite lifecycle usage, and pointer comparison mistakes.

prompt_templates.title: Choose Assert or Require
prompt_templates.prompt: Write a testify test for a function that parses a configuration. Use require for parsing and nil preconditions, then use assert for expected field values.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Mock
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a testify mock for a Sender interface. Verify one call with a specific email, use a context matcher, and check all expectations.

prompt_templates.title: Convert Tests to a Suite
prompt_templates.prompt: Convert these related Go tests into a testify suite. Use shared database setup, fresh mock state before each test, cleanup hooks, and a working suite launcher.

prompt_templates.title: Test Async Retries
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a testify test for an asynchronous client that retries after a timeout. Use sequential mock returns, EventuallyWithT, collected assertions, and explicit timeout intervals.

output_examples.input: How should a test handle a wrapped ErrNotFound value?
output_examples.output: Use testify ErrorIs to match the wrapped error chain. Reserve equality assertions for values that require exact comparison.

output_examples.input: Why did my mock-based test pass when the dependency was never called?
output: Define the expected method call with an explicit call count.
Run AssertExpectations at the end of the test.
Use a specific matcher when the argument must be validated.

output_examples.input: How should a suite initialize a fresh mock for every test?
output_examples.output: Use SetupTest for per-test state, reserve SetupSuite for shared resources, and include the launcher that calls suite.Run.

best_practices: Use require for setup failures that make later assertions unsafe, and use assert for independent outcomes.
Make mock expectations explicit with suitable matchers, call counts, and final verification.
Keep suite lifecycle responsibilities clear and run testifylint during review or continuous integration.
anti_patterns: Using assert for a nil-sensitive precondition and then dereferencing the failed value.
Comparing wrapped errors with direct equality instead of checking the error chain.
Defining mock expectations without verifying them or creating a suite without its launcher.

faq.question: When should I use require instead of assert?
faq.answer: Use require when failure makes later test code unsafe or misleading. Use assert when independent checks should continue after a failure.

faq.question: How do I check a wrapped Go error?
faq.answer: Use ErrorIs with the returned error and target error. It follows wrapped error chains and avoids brittle direct equality.

faq.question: How do I verify a mock call count?
faq.answer: Add Once or Times to the expectation, then call AssertExpectations after exercising the code under test.

faq.question: What matcher ignores an argument value?
faq.answer: Use mock.Anything for broad matching or AnythingOfType when the argument type must still be constrained.

faq.question: How do testify suites run?
faq.answer: Define suite methods, add lifecycle hooks as needed, and create a TestXxx function that calls suite.Run with the suite instance.

faq.question: Can this skill replace testify documentation?
faq.answer: No. It provides practical patterns, but package documentation remains the authority for version-specific APIs and behavior.
